Figure  4  illustrates the distinct circularity paths of hydrogen fuel cell (H 2 FC) and battery electric vehicle (BEV) systems, highlighting how each technology addresses material recovery and reuse within a circular economy framework. For HFCs, the cycle focuses on recovering high-value materials, such as platinum, from fuel cell stacks; however, challenges remain with tank recyclability and component remanufacturing. Conversely, BEVs provide more varied circularity options, including well-established battery recycling methods and promising second-life uses in stationary energy storage. Both systems aim to reduce reliance on virgin raw materials, such as lithium, cobalt, and carbon composites, by reintegrating recovered parts into the production process. Figure  4  illustrates how these technologies can support more sustainable, closed-loop vehicle lifecycles when backed by robust infrastructure and effective policy.

While the circular economy (CE) framework is often promoted as a pathway to sustainability, recent studies highlight that it also entails notable disadvantages and limitations. For example, the rebound effects of CE practices, such as increased production or consumption resulting from efficiency gains, can offset the intended environmental benefits. Additionally, CE strategies such as recycling and remanufacturing often require significant energy inputs and advanced infrastructure, which may compromise their overall potential for carbon reduction. The complexity of global supply chains can further constrain CE implementation, as ensuring full traceability and circularity across different regions remains difficult. Social and economic challenges are also relevant: CE models may create inequalities between countries with advanced technological capabilities and those lacking resources, reinforcing dependency structures. CE should not be viewed as a universal solution, since its benefits are highly context-dependent and may even conflict with other sustainability goals when pursued uncritically [ 222 ,  223 ].

sections.heading: Integrated techno-economic and environmental analysis
paragraphs: Although the primary scope of this study is LCA, a brief discussion on techno-economic aspects in detailed in this section to provide an integrated perspective. This is not intended as a full TEA, but rather as a contextual complement to the environmental results, highlighting where economic factors may influence sustainability outcomes.

The integration of techno-economic and environmental analyses in the manufacturing of fuel cells and batteries is crucial for advancing sustainable energy solutions. Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) and compressed air energy storage (CAES) systems, when thermally integrated, provide a cost-competitive and resilient solution for base-load power generation, particularly in grids with high penetration of variable renewable energy (VRE). This hybrid system maximizes power output during peak demand and stores energy during low demand, enhancing grid stability and reducing carbon emissions [ 224 ,  225 ]. In the automotive sector, fuel cell vehicles (FCVs) are evaluated against battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) for their potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions without the range and refueling limitations of BEVs [ 226 ]. The techno-economic analysis of off-grid hybrid renewable energy systems (HRES) for rural electrification demonstrates the cost-effectiveness and reliability of integrating photovoltaic, wind, biomass, biogas, fuel cells, and battery storage, achieving a cost of energy (COE) of 0.214 USD/kWh. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are pivotal in energy transitions, with their price projected to decrease to 75.1/kWh by 2030, although carbon pricing could offset these reductions. Effective recycling is essential to minimize their carbon footprint and maintain economic viability [ 227 ]. Redox flow batteries, with their low-cost active materials, are promising for long-duration energy storage, supporting the integration of renewable energy into the grid [ 228 ]. The production of green hydrogen through power-to-X processes offers an economically and environmentally viable solution for surplus energy in manufacturing, with hydrogen serving as an energy storage medium, fuel for mobility, and direct use, achieving significant cost reductions and environmental benefits [ 229 ]. These studies collectively underscore the importance of integrating techno-economic and environmental considerations in the development and optimization of fuel cell and battery technologies, ensuring their sustainability and competitiveness in the evolving energy landscape.

sections.heading: Techno-economic assessment overview for an electric vehicle
paragraphs: The techno-economic assessment of electric vehicles (EVs) involves evaluating various financial metrics such as Capital Expenditure (CapEx), Operational Expenditure (OpEx), levelized cost of storage (LCOS), and cost per kWh/km. CapEx for EV infrastructure primarily includes the costs associated with retrofitting existing fuel stations with Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE), integrating Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), and potentially adding photovoltaic (PV) systems to reduce grid connection costs by up to 90% [ 230 ]. Operational Expenditure (OpEx) involves ongoing costs such as maintenance and energy costs, which can be optimized through strategies like Vehicle-to-Home (V2H) operations and Time-of-Use (TOU) tariffs, reducing the economic balance point for EV adoption [ 231 ]. The levelized cost of storage (LCOS) is a critical metric for assessing the economic viability of energy storage solutions, such as flow batteries and V2G technologies, with LCOS for V2G ranging from 00.085/kWh to 0.243/kWh [ 229 ,  232 ]. The cost per kWh/km is influenced by factors such as battery technology and energy efficiency, with advancements in battery technology, such as the transition from Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) to Lithium-Iron-Phosphate (LFP) batteries, aiming to enhance thermal stability and reduce costs [ 233 ]. Additionally, integrating distributed energy resources (DERs) with EV charging stations can significantly reduce local grid usage and improve economic feasibility, although initial investment and maintenance costs remain challenges [ 234 ]. The economic benefits of such integrations are evident in scenarios where energy storage is used to mitigate grid congestion, with profitability increasing as storage costs decrease [ 235 ]. Overall, the techno-economic assessment of EVs and their infrastructure is a complex interplay of various factors, including technological advancements, energy storage solutions, and strategic operational models, all aimed at reducing costs and enhancing the economic viability of EV adoption [ 236 ,  237 – 238 ].

sections.heading: Coupled LCA and TEA frameworks for an EV
paragraphs: The integration of LCA and Techno-Economic Assessment (TEA) frameworks for EVs provides a comprehensive approach to evaluating their environmental and economic impacts. LCA studies, such as those by Helmers et al., emphasize the importance of real-world data in assessing the environmental benefits of converting ICEVs to EVs, highlighting a 16% reduction in CO 2 -equivalent emissions when using real-world energy consumption data [ 55 ] (Helmers et al., 2017). Similarly, Zimmermann et al. [ 239 ] underscore the significance of incorporating dynamic changes in electricity supply, such as Germany’s Energiewende, into LCA to better predict future environmental impacts of EVs. The integration of energy flow modeling in LCA, as discussed by Schulz-Mönninghoff et al., [ 240 ] further enhances the assessment by evaluating the repurposing of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in a circular economy context, revealing that multi-use cases can reduce climate change benefits by 10–22% compared to single applications. Tagliaferri et al. [ 81 ] provide a cradle-to-grave LCA approach, identifying the manufacturing phase of EVs as a significant environmental burden due to the use of metals in battery packs, although the use phase of EVs results in significantly lower greenhouse gas emissions compared to ICEVs. On the economic front, Ghosh et al. [ 230 ] explore the techno-economic feasibility of retrofitting existing fuel stations with EV charging infrastructure, finding that configurations with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and photovoltaic systems can significantly reduce grid connection costs. The importance of the electricity mix in LCA is further highlighted by Girardi et al., who demonstrate that despite a fossil fuel-dominated power mix, EVs in Italy still outperform ICEVs in reducing air acidification and greenhouse gases [ 241 ]. The economic viability of recycling and remanufacturing LIBs is explored by Choux et al. [ 201 ] and Kamath et al., [ 242 ] who find that automated disassembly and remanufacturing can enhance material recovery and reduce the carbon footprint, although economic incentives may be necessary to maintain profitability as battery prices decrease. Alfaro-Algaba and Ramirez [ 205 ] present a model for optimizing the disassembly of EV battery packs, emphasizing the economic and environmental benefits of remanufacturing and recycling. Together, these studies demonstrate the crucial role of integrated LCA and TEA frameworks in promoting sustainable electric mobility by considering both environmental impacts and economic feasibility.

Covering passenger EVs, electric buses, and infrastructure like charging stations, these studies offer valuable insights into how economic feasibility and environmental sustainability intersect across different regions and electricity mixes. sections.heading: Optimization strategies–trade-offs between cost, emissions, and resource use
paragraphs: Optimization strategies for EVs involve balancing trade-offs between cost, emissions, and resource use, which are critical for enhancing their adoption and efficiency. A key strategy is the implementation of adaptive supervisory control in plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), which optimizes power-split and air path settings to minimize operational costs and emissions, achieving reductions of up to 10% in cost and 22% in emissions in real-world cycles [ 252 ]. Variable engine calibration (VEC) further enhances this trade-off by optimizing fuel consumption and NOx emissions, with simulations showing a 5.4% reduction in fuel consumption at equivalent NOx levels for conventional vehicles, and significant NOx reductions for hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) [ 253 ]. Meta-heuristic optimization techniques, including swarm-intelligent and evolutionary algorithms, are also pivotal in improving EV technologies by addressing design, energy management, and charging strategies, thus reducing greenhouse emissions and enhancing range and cost efficiency [ 254 ]. Lifecycle analysis reveals that HEVs are often the most cost-effective choice for high vehicle miles traveled (VMT), while PHEVs are optimal for minimizing lifecycle emissions across various VMT levels [ 255 ]. Effective charge scheduling is essential to manage the unpredictable load of EVs on the grid, with optimization techniques ensuring harmony among consumers, aggregators, and utility services [ 256 ](Salam et al., 2024). Multi-objective optimization models for route planning consider travel costs, energy consumption, and charging costs, using genetic algorithms to provide feasible route advice that balances these factors [ 257 ]. Energy-efficiency-driven route optimization, such as the green waveband (GWB) model, further reduces energy consumption and travel time, offering a trade-off between energy use and time cost [ 258 ]. The strategic allocation of public charging stations in urban networks can minimize greenhouse gas emissions and user costs, with optimal solutions closely aligning with emission-minimizing policies [ 259 ]. Finally, addressing battery degradation through counter-aging control strategies can extend battery life and driving range, demonstrating the potential of integrated optimization approaches to enhance EV performance while maintaining drivability [ 260 ]. These strategies collectively emphasize the importance of a multifaceted approach to optimize cost, emissions, and resource utilization in EVs.

It should be noted that a comprehensive techno-economic assessment (TEA) would require an expanded methodological framework beyond the present study’s LCA scope. Future work should explore integrated LCA–TEA frameworks in greater depth, as they can offer a more holistic view of FCEVs and BEVs technologies.

sections.heading: Emerging innovations and future research directions
paragraphs: Emerging innovations in the manufacturing of fuel cells and batteries for EVs are pivotal for advancing sustainable transportation. Fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) are gaining traction due to their high efficiency, zero emissions, and long driving range, with proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) and solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) being the most promising technologies. Recent advancements in PEMFCs, such as the incorporation of carbon nanotubes and graphene oxide into membranes, have significantly enhanced performance, although challenges like cost and durability remain [ 261 ,  262 ]. The integration of power electronic systems in FCEVs, including high-voltage DC/DC converters and energy management systems, is crucial for optimizing performance and efficiency [ 263 ]. On the battery front, the European Commission’s Battery 2030 + initiative emphasizes the need for ultra-high-performance batteries that surpass current lithium-ion technologies in terms of cost, reliability, and sustainability [ 264 ]. Innovations in battery technology, such as model-driven manufacturing approaches, are being explored to enhance energy density, safety, and cost-effectiveness, with computational models playing a key role in optimizing manufacturing processes [ 265 ]. The development of high-energy-density batteries is essential for meeting the demands of long-range and high-utilization EV markets, which are not fully served by existing lithium-ion batteries [ 266 ]. Moreover, the environmental impact of lithium-ion batteries is a concern, necessitating advancements in recycling and second-life applications to ensure sustainability [ 27 ]. The future of EVs also hinges on the integration of autonomous and connected vehicle technologies, which require robust energy management and battery optimization strategies [ 267 ]. Interdisciplinary collaboration and innovation are critical to overcoming the technical and environmental challenges in the manufacturing of fuel cells and batteries, paving the way for a cleaner and more efficient transportation future [ 268 ].

sections.heading: Novel materials & architectures: solid-state batteries, graphene membranes, H 2  carriers
paragraphs: Emerging innovations in EV energy storage are significantly advancing through the development of solid-state batteries (SSBs), graphene membranes, and solid-state hydrogen carriers. Solid-state batteries, particularly those using solid electrolytes, are at the forefront due to their potential for higher energy density, improved safety, and longer cycle life compared to traditional lithium-ion batteries. However, challenges such as low ionic conductivity, mechanical degradation, and manufacturing complexities persist, necessitating ongoing research into materials and interfaces to enhance performance and stability [ 269 ,  270 – 271 ]. Recent advancements include the development of ultrathin solid electrolyte membranes, which offer improved mechanical robustness and ionic conductivity, thereby enhancing the energy density of all-solid-state batteries (ASBs) [ 272 ]. Additionally, innovations in manufacturing techniques, such as physical vapor deposition, are facilitating the precise fabrication of battery components, contributing to better understanding and optimization of material properties and interfacial phenomena [ 273 ]. In parallel, solid-state hydrogen storage technologies are gaining traction as a viable solution for high-density energy storage, with research focusing on nanostructure design to optimize kinetics and thermodynamics. This includes the use of magnesium-based and vanadium-based materials, which promise high safety and energy density, potentially transforming hydrogen storage into a mainstream technology within the next decade [ 274 ,  275 ]. These advancements are complemented by the exploration of graphene membranes, which, although not explicitly detailed in the provided contexts, are known for their exceptional conductivity and mechanical properties, making them a promising candidate for enhancing the performance of both batteries and hydrogen storage systems. These innovations are poised to significantly impact the EV industry by providing more efficient, safe, and sustainable energy storage solutions, thereby supporting the broader transition to clean energy technologies [ 276 ,  277 – 278 ].

sections.heading: Digital twins & AI for LCA: maintenance prediction & resource optimization
paragraphs: The integration of Digital Twins (DTs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing offers significant potential for optimizing life cycle assessment (LCA) through predictive maintenance and smart resource allocation. Digital Twins provide a real-time, cyber-physical representation of manufacturing entities, enabling precise monitoring and predictive capabilities that are crucial for maintenance and resource management [ 279 ,  280 ]. Predictive maintenance, facilitated by DTs, allows for the calculation of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of machinery, thus preventing unexpected downtimes and reducing overhaul costs [ 281 ,  282 ]. The use of AI, particularly machine learning models like Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), enhances the predictive accuracy of these systems, as demonstrated by the FUCOM-ANN model, which significantly reduces prediction errors compared to traditional methods [ 283 ]. In the context of EVs, DTs are employed to optimize battery management systems by accurately predicting the state of charge and health, which is vital for battery efficiency and longevity [ 284 ]. However, the complexity of data dependencies and constraints in manufacturing processes poses challenges to the accuracy of AI models, necessitating the development of dependency/constraint-aware models [ 280 ]. Moreover, the integration of cloud-edge-device collaboration in DTs can improve communication efficiency and resource allocation, further enhancing the sustainability of manufacturing operations [ 285 ]. Despite these advancements, challenges such as the computational burden and data variety remain, highlighting the need for continued research and development in this field [ 282 ]. Overall, the synergy between DTs and AI in EV manufacturing not only supports predictive maintenance but also facilitates smart resource allocation, contributing to more efficient and sustainable production systems.

sections.heading: Policy & regulatory trends: eu battery directive, IRA, circularity mandates
paragraphs: The European Union’s battery regulations, particularly the EU Battery Directive and the recent Regulation 2023/1542, are pivotal in shaping the electric vehicle (EV) sector’s transition towards a circular economy. These regulations emphasize the full lifecycle management of batteries, aiming to enhance sustainability by integrating circular economy principles into the battery supply chain [ 286 ,  287 ]. The EU’s approach involves a shift from directives to more stringent regulations, which exert pressure on stakeholders to adopt sustainable practices, focusing on operational sustainability, research and development, and collaborative dynamics [ 287 ]. The regulations also address the environmental and social impacts of battery production, particularly the upstream processes of mining and manufacturing, which are significant sources of greenhouse gas emissions [ 288 ,  289 ]. The EU’s regulatory framework aims to mitigate these impacts by mandating carbon footprint declarations and setting upper limits for emissions from battery production [ 289 ]. Moreover, the EU’s policies are designed to foster innovation and collaboration among stakeholders, encouraging the development of circular business models that promote battery reuse and recycling [ 47 ,  219 ]. However, challenges remain, such as the need for more detailed incentives and the broad classification of economic operators, which could lead to competitive imbalances [ 287 ]. The EU’s regulatory efforts are part of a broader strategy to achieve climate neutrality by 2050, with electric vehicles playing a crucial role in reducing transport-related emissions [ 290 ,  291 ]. The Inflation Reduction Act in the United States complements these efforts by providing financial incentives for clean energy technologies, including EVs, thereby supporting the global transition to sustainable transportation [ 292 ]. Together, these policies and regulations underscore the importance of aligning economic and environmental interests to create a sustainable and competitive battery ecosystem in Europe and beyond [ 286 ,  292 ].

sections.heading: Recommendations and strategic roadmap
Industry actions: best practices, circular KPIs & supplier engagement
paragraphs: The strategic roadmap for the EV industry encompasses a multifaceted approach that incorporates best practices, key performance indicators (KPIs) focused on circularity, and supplier engagement. Best practices in the EV supply chain emphasize the transformation of supplier roles and the importance of collaboration between suppliers and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to maintain competitiveness in the evolving landscape [ 33 ]. Circular KPIs are crucial for assessing the sustainability of EVs, with a focus on renewable energy use and recycled materials, as demonstrated by the circular economy framework applied to Ford Motor Company’s sustainability initiatives [ 44 ]. The integration of circular business models, such as extending, sharing, and looping, is essential for achieving battery circularity, which is a critical component of the EV ecosystem [ 219 ]. Supplier engagement plays a pivotal role in reducing Scope 3 emissions, with strategies such as effective communication, trust-building, and supplier incentive programs being identified as effective methods to engage suppliers in emission reduction efforts [ 305 ]. Additionally, the adoption of circular supply chains (CSCs) is highlighted as a key enabler for closing resource loops and maximizing value recovery, with a guiding framework proposed to manage the complexities of CSC implementation [ 215 ]. The transition towards a circular economy in the automotive industry also involves promoting new green technologies and extending product life cycles, which are vital for minimizing resource functionality loss [ 306 ]. Moreover, the digitalization of supply chains, driven by smart work environments and data-driven process optimization, supports the integration of circular economy principles, enhancing the sustainability of the supply chain network [ 307 ]. The strategic roadmap for the EV industry requires a comprehensive approach that integrates circular economy practices, robust supplier engagement, and innovative business models to achieve sustainability and emission reduction goals.

sections.heading: Research gaps–data quality, regional differences, end-of-life tracking
paragraphs: Research on EVs reveals significant gaps in data quality, regional variability, and EoL tracking, which are critical for understanding and improving the sustainability of EVs. Regional variability in life cycle CO 2  emissions is a significant concern, as studies have shown that emissions estimates can vary substantially depending on the regional electricity grid’s emission factors and boundaries used for analysis. For example, when applying state-level versus National Electricity Reliability Commission (NERC) regional boundaries, life cycle emission estimates for the same location can differ by as much as 120%. This discrepancy underscores not a lack of data availability, but rather the sensitivity of LCA results to boundary definitions and modeling choices. While regional electricity production data is generally available, which helps to improve the accuracy of assessments, some variability in results will always remain for EVs due to temporal changes in the electricity mix, differences in grid carbon intensity, and variations in charging patterns [ 308 ]. Additionally, the lack of harmonized data on transport behavior across regions, particularly in Europe, poses a bottleneck for tracking progress towards sustainable transport goals. This gap underscores the necessity for coordinated data collection efforts, such as surveys and mobile data, to monitor shifts towards more sustainable transport modes [ 309 ]. At the EoL phase, the transportation and recycling of EV batteries present logistical and environmental challenges. The literature indicates that transportation costs for EoL batteries can vary widely, and the environmental impact of transporting these batteries contributes to a small but significant portion of their life cycle emissions [ 310 ]. Moreover, the dynamic stockpile of lithium-ion batteries at EoL presents technical and policy challenges that need to be addressed to manage the economic and environmental costs associated with battery waste [ 35 ]. The variability in data quality and the lack of comprehensive data on battery health and EoL management highlight the need for improved data-driven approaches and standardized methodologies to enhance the accuracy of life cycle assessments and inform sustainable policy-making [ 57 ,  311 ]. Addressing these research gaps is crucial for optimizing the environmental benefits of EVs and ensuring their role in a sustainable transportation future.

sections.heading: Policy suggestions–incentives for design-for-reuse, recycling infrastructure
paragraphs: To effectively promote the design-for-reuse and recycling infrastructure for EVs, a multifaceted approach involving policy incentives and infrastructure development is essential. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) legislation can play a crucial role by incentivizing producers to design products with recyclability in mind, although collective EPR systems may offer less motivation for individual design improvements compared to individual systems [ 312 ]. In the context of ELVs, the EU’s directive on ELVs emphasizes the need for advanced recycling technologies, such as automobile shredder residue (ASR) recovery, which can enhance recycling rates and meet regulatory targets [ 313 ]. For EV batteries, implementing reward–penalty and deposit–refund mechanisms can significantly improve collection rates and recycling enterprise profits, with the deposit–refund mechanism generally yielding higher collection rates [ 314 ]. Additionally, the development of a robust recycling network, as demonstrated in Xi’an, China, can optimize the reverse logistics process and enhance economic and environmental benefits [ 315 ]. Financial and non-financial incentives also play a critical role in EV adoption and infrastructure development. Financial subsidies have been shown to increase EV sales and market share, while non-financial incentives, such as parking benefits and lane access, further boost adoption [ 316 ,  317 ]. Moreover, the strategic allocation of rebates and charging infrastructure investments can optimize EV adoption and emission reductions, with rebates being more effective for modest drivers and charging stations prioritized for frequent drivers [ 318 ]. Policymakers should consider the indirect network and herd effects when designing subsidy policies, as these can influence the effectiveness of consumer and infrastructure firm subsidies [ 319 ]. A comprehensive policy framework that integrates design incentives, recycling infrastructure, and both financial and non-financial incentives is crucial for advancing the sustainability of the EV industry.

sections.heading: Integrated LCA framework: comparing hydrogen vs. battery electric vehicles
paragraphs: Fig. 6 Proposed integrated comparative LCA framework for HFCV and BEV under sustainability criteria

Figure  6  shows a detailed conceptual framework created to guide the comparative LCA of HFCVs and BEVs within the context of sustainable mobility. The framework begins by identifying the two primary systems under analysis: HFCVs and BEVs. These lead into three important LCA stages such as production, use, and EoL. During the production phase, it considers the extraction of raw materials, energy use in manufacturing, and related emissions. The use phase covers vehicle operation, including fuel or electricity consumption, efficiency, and emissions during driving. The EoL phase examines disposal methods, recycling efficiency, and the potential for second-life applications.

Alongside the lifecycle stages, the framework includes a set of evaluation criteria: environmental impact (e.g., GHG emissions, energy use), economic performance (e.g., lifecycle cost, infrastructure needs), and circularity (e.g., material recovery, reuse). These indicators help assess the overall sustainability and feasibility of each technology. Additionally, the model incorporates key cross-cutting factors such as the energy source mix (e.g., fossil-based versus renewable electricity or hydrogen), policy and regulatory influences (e.g., subsidies, mandates, and emissions targets), technological maturity, and regional differences, which can significantly affect LCA results.

At the bottom of the framework, comparative insights summarize the strengths and limitations of each vehicle type. BEVs are recognized for their low operational emissions and well-established recycling infrastructure, but face challenges related to raw material sourcing and high manufacturing impacts. HFCVs offer advantages such as faster refueling and more extended range, but are currently hindered by high hydrogen production emissions and limited EoL strategies. This conceptual framework provides a structured and transparent method for researchers, policymakers, and industry stakeholders to evaluate and compare the lifecycle performance of emerging vehicle technologies in a reproducible and scalable way.

sections.heading: Modeling BEVs and FCEVs with prospective LCA
paragraphs: While the present review synthesizes largely retrospective LCAs, prospective LCA (pLCA) approaches are increasingly recognized as a critical complement [ 320 ,  321 ]. pLCA provides a powerful lens for evaluating the future environmental performance of BEVs and FCEVs within decarbonization trajectories. Such methods, which integrate scenario analysis, dynamic inventories, and energy system projections, can clarify how future grid decarbonization, hydrogen production pathways, and advanced battery chemistries may shift the relative impacts of BEVs and FCEVs [ 320 ,  321 ]. Recent study by Šimaitis et al., [ 320 ] illustrate that couple LCA with long-term energy transition scenarios helps anticipate how scaling and technology innovation may reshape environmental trade-offs. Recent research by Xue et al. [ 322 ] applied a pLCA integrated with vehicle dynamic simulation to compare heavy-duty truck powertrains, BEV, FCEV, and hydrogen combustion under China’s evolving freight and energy landscapes. Their results show that decarbonizing both electricity grids and hydrogen supply chains by 2035 could reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by over 55% for all technologies. However, suitability varies with context: BEVs are optimal for regional routes, while FCEVs suit long-haul, low-load applications. In parallel, Khadhraoui and Adnen [ 323 ] demonstrated a vehicle prototype utilizing on-board hydrogen production powered by solar and lithium-ion systems. Their proton-exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) achieved a 98% CO 2  reduction compared to conventional engines, illustrating the substantial future gains possible with integrated renewable energy and hydrogen technologies. Wang [ 324 ] contextualizes these innovations within a broader automotive landscape, emphasizing that the evolution of BEVs and FCEVs must account for infrastructure, battery constraints, and fuel supply transitions. pLCA facilitates this by modeling not only end-use emissions but also the dynamic interplay between technological advancements and regulatory shifts, offering a roadmap for achieving net-zero mobility goals. In regions with a high proportion of renewable energy, BEVs can achieve up to 90% CO 2  emissions reduction compared to ICEVs, underscoring the importance of regional energy policies in maximizing the benefits of EVs [ 325 ]. Overall, while BEVs currently offer superior environmental and economic advantages over FCEVs, the future potential of both technologies will depend on advancements in energy infrastructure, battery technology, and regional energy policies.

sections.heading: Concluding remarks
paragraphs: This review set out to comprehensively assess the environmental sustainability of HFCVs and BEVs through the lens of LCA. As the global transportation sector rapidly shifts toward decarbonization, evaluating these emerging technologies holistically rather than just at the tailpipe across their entire life cycles has become more critical than ever. Drawing from a wide range of peer-reviewed studies, technical reports, and literature that utilize recognized LCA databases, this review has unpacked the trade-offs, challenges, and opportunities that both hydrogen and battery systems present for the future of clean mobility.

One of the key takeaways is that neither HFCVs nor BEVs offer a universally superior environmental profile; instead, their relative performance varies greatly depending on lifecycle stage, regional energy mix, and assumptions about technology development. In the production phase, BEVs typically exhibit higher environmental burdens, primarily due to the extraction and processing of critical raw materials, such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel, used in battery production. However, this impact can be partially mitigated by advances in battery chemistry (e.g., LFP or sodium-ion alternatives), improved mining practices, and more energy-efficient manufacturing processes. HFCVs, in contrast, tend to have lower upfront material-related impacts but face significant energy and emissions challenges in the hydrogen production stage, mainly when hydrogen is derived from fossil sources (e.g., steam methane reforming).

In the use phase, BEVs generally outperform HFCVs in terms of GHG emissions and energy efficiency, primarily because electric drivetrains are inherently more efficient, and electricity generation, especially in regions with high renewable energy penetration, can be relatively clean. HFCVs, while offering advantages in refueling time and driving range, are disadvantaged by the lower round-trip efficiency of hydrogen and the current carbon intensity of hydrogen supply chains. That said, the performance gap may narrow as green hydrogen production via electrolysis using renewable electricity becomes more widespread, with literature indicating that continued technological improvements, cost reductions in renewable energy, and economies of scale are likely to improve its cost-competitiveness relative to conventional alternatives.

The EoL phase remains a critical area of uncertainty and opportunity for both technologies. Battery recycling is evolving rapidly, supported by policy initiatives in the EU, China, and the U.S., but it still faces challenges related to scalability, safety, and economics. On the hydrogen side, while fuel cells are generally modular and easier to disassemble, the recovery of materials such as platinum-group metals is not yet standardized at scale. Both pathways would benefit significantly from design-for-disassembly strategies and more circular business models that promote reuse, refurbishment, and materials recovery.

Another important insight from this review is that context matters greatly. The environmental performance and the cost-related implications of each technology, as reported in the literature, are influenced by local and regional factors such as the energy mix, policy incentives, infrastructure availability, and consumer behaviour. For example, BEVs exhibit significantly greater emissions savings in countries with a green electricity grid. In contrast, HFCVs may prove more viable in sectors or regions where long-range, heavy-duty transport and rapid refueling are key priorities.

From a policy and planning perspective, the review suggests that a diversified approach may be the most pragmatic route forward. Rather than framing BEVs and HFCVs as competing technologies, they can be viewed as complementary, each suited to different use cases. Recent research demonstrates that BEVs are no longer limited to urban and light-duty applications; with the emergence of megawatt charging systems and falling battery costs, they are becoming increasingly viable for regional and even long-haul freight transport. HFCVs, meanwhile, may remain important in specific contexts such as grid-constrained regions, high-utilization fleets requiring rapid turnaround, or applications with extreme payload and range demands, but their future role will depend heavily on the availability of low-carbon hydrogen and supporting infrastructure.

Despite its comprehensive scope, this review also acknowledges a few limitations. First, there is a lack of standardization across LCA studies, which often use different system boundaries, functional units, and data sources, making direct comparisons difficult. To move beyond this limitation, it is recommended (i) to promote greater transparency by requiring LCAs to report assumptions, boundary choices, and datasets in a harmonized template; (ii) to reinforce the consistent application of sector-specific functional units, for example, per tonne-km for freight transport and per passenger-km for passenger transport, not as new methodological concepts but as essential practices that are still applied inconsistently in current studies, particularly in emerging areas such as hydrogen fuel cells and next-generation battery systems; (iii) to adopt open-access LCA databases that align with region-specific energy mixes; and (iv) to develop methodological approaches that integrate standardization with structured flexibility by designing modular LCA frameworks that maintain a standardized core structure including consistent system boundaries, reporting formats, and impact categories while allowing additional components to adapt to variations in regional energy mixes, emerging technologies, and evolving policy contexts. Incorporating dynamic LCA models that capture temporal changes such as grid decarbonization or technological progress, and ensuring transparent documentation of any deviations from standard practices, can further enhance robustness, comparability, and policy relevance without compromising adaptability. These measures are intended to enhance comparability, reproducibility, and policy relevance while avoiding the pitfalls of rigid one-size-fits-all methodologies. Second, there is still limited empirical data for many next-generation technologies, such as solid-state batteries or decentralized green hydrogen production. Third, the field needs more real-world lifecycle data across different geographies to supplement lab-based assumptions. These gaps highlight the importance of harmonized methodologies, open LCA databases, and transparent reporting standards to ensure consistency and comparability in future research.

Looking ahead, several promising research directions emerge. While prospective and dynamic LCAs have already been developed to capture changing grid mixes, temporal variations, and evolving technology pathways, there remains significant scope to refine and expand their application. Integrating temporal LCA with region-specific energy transitions, battery second-life applications, and future hydrogen deployment scenarios will provide even more nuanced and realistic assessments. Furthermore, extending these analyses beyond environmental dimensions to explicitly incorporate techno-economic perspectives, behavioral adoption patterns, and systems-level modeling can create a more comprehensive framework for sustainability.

Moreover, policy instruments such as carbon pricing, extended producer responsibility, and green procurement can further accelerate the deployment of low-impact technologies. By combining methodological advances in prospective LCA with supportive policies and circular design principles, both BEVs and HFCVs can be evaluated more robustly in terms of their long-term contributions to climate goals. This review emphasizes the importance of life cycle thinking not just as a static accounting framework, but as an evolving, context-sensitive tool to guide sustainable mobility transitions in a rapidly decarbonizing world.

Ultimately, it is crucial to acknowledge that vehicle-level efficiency improvements, whether in BEVs or HFCVs, cannot entirely offset the effects of an overall car-dependent mobility paradigm. Complementary strategies such as reducing vehicle mass, promoting shared mobility, and strengthening public transportation systems can yield substantially greater environmental benefits by addressing mobility demand at the system level. In conclusion, this review highlights the importance of life cycle thinking in promoting sustainable mobility transitions. While BEVs and HFCVs both hold transformative potential, their environmental value depends on how and where they are produced, used, and retired. With the right mix of technological innovation, supportive policies, and circular design, both technologies can make meaningful contributions to global climate and sustainability goals. This review synthesizes the current state of knowledge and identifies methodological priorities, thereby contributing to the development of more integrated and context-sensitive LCAs in future research.

sections.heading: Limitations
paragraphs: While this review has sought to provide a comprehensive assessment of BEVs and HFCVs using life cycle approaches, certain impact categories were not explicitly addressed. In particular, non-exhaust emissions such as particulate matter (PM) from brake, tire, and road wear, as well as emerging concerns such as microplastic pollution, were excluded from the scope. The main reason for this omission is the lack of consistent methodologies and harmonized datasets across LCA studies, which makes systematic comparison difficult. However, these impacts are increasingly recognized as critical for evaluating the true environmental burden of transportation systems. Future work should therefore integrate these categories using standardized metrics, improved modeling frameworks, and more complete datasets to enable more holistic and comparable assessments.

It is also important to acknowledge that while this review has aimed to provide a holistic evaluation of BEVs and HFCVs through LCA, certain aspects such as the regional techno-economic feasibility of hydrogen pathways and broader socio-environmental considerations (e.g., air quality co-benefits, particulate emissions, and alternative mobility options) remain outside its immediate scope. These dimensions warrant deeper exploration in future research to complement the findings presented here.
